messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elias Vance had driven the number forty-two route for twenty years before the summer layover fractured his routine. After fourteen hours of navigating gridlock, he had pulled into the abandoned transfer point, his body aching with a bone-deep exhaustion that made his hands tremble on the wheel. He had never expected vulnerability to find him in a place he considered neutral, but when the depot gate clanged shut, the sharp metallic echo trapped him before he could react. The violation was sudden and absolute. What frightened him most was the immediate dawning conviction that people could not be trusted and that he had lost his faith in any higher power to intervene. Over the following months, his mind began to hoard the assault like a damaged reel. He told his wife it played like a broken film, forcing him to sit in the dark until the terror he felt at the time fully collapsed into a profound shame that made him feel permanently marked. The fatigue that once signaled a routine shift now acted as a direct gateway to his trauma. When Elias pushed through his final stops, his eyelids growing heavy, that familiar exhaustion would immediately pull the assault into focus. He would find himself gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles whitened, the physical tiredness instantly unlocking the vivid, unspooled replay of the attack. The moment his body registered weariness, his mind could not help but drag him back to the exact second the hands had closed over him, turning a simple commute into a recurring reenactment. That same exhaustion, combined with the weight of carrying passengers, quickly solidified his growing conviction that the world was fundamentally broken. When he was forced to drive with others during crowded rush hour, the proximity of strangers immediately sharpened his belief that people could not be trusted. He stopped making eye contact, interpreting their glances through the lens of his own diminished worth. The daily reality of the bus route stopped being a job and became a continuous test of his suspicion; every distant siren and every tired passenger reinforced his certainty that he had lost his faith in life and in his own safety among them. His deepening suspicion did not just shape his daily interactions; it actively dictated how his past resurfaced. Because he had come to believe that he could not rely on anyone, his mind began to curate his flashbacks with ruthless severity. Every time the film of the assault rolled to its climax, his negative appraisal of the world flooded in, amplifying the intense shame he felt when recalling the event. He stopped fighting the memories, convinced that his body had been permanently defiled. The appraisal of universal untrustworthiness acted as a lens, turning neutral recollections into relentless confirmations of his own bodily disgrace. This entrenched pessimism did not stay confined to his thoughts; it actively recruited his environment into his suffering. His conviction that people were inherently dangerous made the mere presence of other commuters feel like an active threat. He began taking longer, darker routes to avoid shared stops, his mistrust transforming routine transit into a landscape of potential ambush. When the depot’s security cameras buzzed or the brake hydraulics hissed, his belief that he had lost his faith left him feeling utterly exposed, stripping away any buffer against the noise. His negative worldview did not just coexist with his triggers; it sharpened them, ensuring that every sound and every ache would instantly signal impending danger. The cycle tightened when the memories themselves began to manufacture new points of entry. The unspooled film of the assault no longer waited for him to rest; it began to project its own demands onto his waking hours. When the replay brought back the same terror he felt at the time, his nervous system would hijack his routine, forcing him to abandon shifts the moment he felt even mildly fatigued. He could no longer tolerate driving with others, because the phantom weight of the attack would suddenly surface, making the driver’s seat feel like a trap. The memory did not just return; it actively generated a new set of alarms, ensuring that fatigue and passenger proximity would forever be linked to the violation. Now, Elias sits in his small apartment, the radio quietly static, waiting for a clinician who might finally help him untangle the knot in his chest. He has not driven a city bus in eight months, and his wife, Claire, walks on eggshells around his sudden insomnia and the way he flinches at the hum of the refrigerator. He came to the intake hoping to reclaim some fragment of the man he was, but what frightens him most is the fear that the loop is permanent. He worries that if he ever steps back behind the wheel, or if his body simply gives out from exhaustion, the film will start again without warning.
